issues.legal_issue: A final judgment of the highest court cannot be reopened through repeated interlocutory applications after review and curative remedies have failed, absent exceptional circumstances warranting recall.
material_facts: The court had finally determined the industries’ environmental liability and ordered remediation costs, and subsequent review and curative petitions had been dismissed.
The applicants had been heard in the original proceedings and later filed repeated applications seeking to challenge the findings and avoid compliance.
The applications relied on later expert reports and renewed allegations about earlier reports, but did not establish a qualifying exceptional ground for reopening the judgment.
issues.conclusion: The applications could not be used to reopen the concluded judgment and were dismissed as an abuse of the process of the court.
issues.legal_principle: Finality of judgments serves the public interest in certainty and an end to litigation. Under Article 141 and the principles discussed in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra, Northern India Caterers (India) Ltd. v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, and M. Nagabhushana v. State of Karnataka, a final judgment is not ordinarily reconsidered merely to reargue concluded matters. Recall may be justified in truly exceptional circumstances, including a serious violation of natural justice or circumstances that undermine public confidence in the administration of justice.

predicates.collateral_challenge_to_final_apex_judgm: The applicant sought through a later collateral proceeding to challenge a final judgment of the highest court.
predicates.review_and_curative_remedies_exhausted: The applicant’s available review and curative proceedings had already been dismissed.
predicates.applicant_received_a_fair_hearing: The applicant had an opportunity to present its case in the proceedings that produced the final judgment.
predicates.no_exceptional_reopening_ground_establis: The applicant did not establish an exceptional circumstance, such as a serious denial of natural justice, that justified reopening the judgment.

issues.definition: When a party that has already received a fair hearing and exhausted review and curative remedies brings a collateral challenge without establishing an exceptional ground, the final judgment remains undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A final remediation liability for environmental harm is not extinguished merely because a liable polluter later asserts that contamination has diminished or disappeared.
material_facts: The court had previously determined that industrial waste caused environmental harm and that the industries were liable for remediation.
The remediation amount and the measures based on expert reports had been accepted in earlier orders.
The applicants later relied on reports obtained at their instance to claim that little or no remediation was currently needed.
The court considered the prior findings and subsequent material and rejected the attempt to use the later claims to avoid the settled liability.
issues.conclusion: The applicants remained liable to pay the previously determined remediation costs, and later claims about the current condition of the environment did not justify reopening that liability.
issues.legal_principle: The polluter-pays principle places the financial costs of preventing or remedying pollution on those responsible for it. Under the absolute-liability principle stated in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (the Oleum Gas Leak case), an enterprise engaged in hazardous activity is liable for harm caused by that activity. The court had applied those principles in its earlier judgment and held the industries liable for restoration; finality principles prevent a later collateral application from relitigating that determination. M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath also recognizes liability for restoration of the environment and ecology.

predicates.environmental_remediation_enforcement_pr: The proceeding concerns enforcement of an existing obligation to remediate environmental harm.
predicates.polluter_liability_previously_finally_de: A final judgment has already found the polluter liable for the environmental harm and remediation.
predicates.later_claim_of_reduced_or_absent_contami: The polluter later claims that contamination has diminished or is no longer present.
predicates.no_exceptional_ground_for_reopening: The later material does not establish an exceptional basis for reopening the final determination.

issues.definition: In an environmental remediation enforcement proceeding, a polluter remains bound to fund remediation when liability was finally determined and later claims about reduced contamination do not establish an exceptional basis to reopen it.

issues.legal_issue: A party that retains money by delaying compliance with a final payment order may be required to pay compound interest as restitution to neutralize the benefit of non-compliance and compensate the creditor.
material_facts: The court had fixed the amount payable toward remediation, and the industry was required to pay it.
The industry did not pay and instead pursued repeated challenges that delayed payment for many years.
The industry retained the use of the unpaid money while the government and affected community were deprived of funds for remedial measures.
The court found that the delayed payment produced an unjust benefit and prevented timely restoration.
issues.conclusion: The industry was ordered to pay compound interest on the remediation amount from the date it became payable until payment or recovery.
issues.legal_principle: Restitution requires the court to neutralize an unfair advantage obtained through delay or non-compliance and to make the deprived party whole. The court relied on the principle that no one may benefit from their own wrong; the restitution decisions in Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer, Kavita Trehan v. Balsara Hygiene Products, and South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. v. State of M.P.; and the recognition of compound interest in appropriate restitution cases discussed in Sempra Metals Ltd. v. Inland Revenue and Bank of America Canada v. Mutual Trust Co. The court held that its inherent powers and principles of justice and equity permit compound interest in a proceeding not governed by a suit for recovery under the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: court_order_enforcement_proceeding and payment_amount_finally_fixed and judgment_debtor_withheld_payment and delay_deprived_creditor_of_use_of_money

predicates.court_order_enforcement_proceeding: The proceeding seeks enforcement of a court order requiring payment.
predicates.payment_amount_finally_fixed: The amount payable under the court’s order has been finally determined.
predicates.judgment_debtor_withheld_payment: The party required to pay did not pay the amount when required.
predicates.delay_deprived_creditor_of_use_of_money: The non-payment deprived the creditor of the use of money needed to carry out the ordered remedial work.

issues.definition: When a party withholds a finally fixed payment and thereby deprives the creditor of its use, the party must pay compound restitution interest in the enforcement proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A party that prolongs litigation through abusive applications to evade a final judgment may be ordered to pay realistic litigation costs.
material_facts: After the final judgment and dismissal of review and curative petitions, the applicants filed further applications seeking to relitigate settled issues and delay payment.
The respondents were compelled to defend the applications, and court time was expended on the prolonged litigation.
The court found the applications devoid of merit and part of an effort to avoid compliance with its orders.
issues.conclusion: The applicants were ordered to pay costs for the litigation, with the costs directed to be used for remedial measures in the affected area.
issues.legal_principle: Courts have a duty to prevent abuse of their process and to neutralize undeserved advantages obtained through delay. Realistic costs may reflect the burden imposed on the opposing parties and may deter dishonest or obstructive litigation. The court relied on Sita Ram Bhandar Society v. Lieutenant Governor, Government of NCT, Delhi, Ramrameshwari Devi v. Nirmala Devi, and the restitution and costs principles discussed in Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer and South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. v. State of M.P.

predicates.court_proceeding_to_enforce_final_judgme: The proceeding concerns enforcement of a final court judgment.
predicates.repeated_meritless_applications_to_delay: A party repeatedly filed applications lacking merit in order to delay compliance with the judgment.
predicates.opposing_parties_forced_to_defend: The repeated applications required the opposing parties to incur the burden of defending the litigation.

issues.definition: When a party repeatedly brings meritless applications to delay compliance with a final judgment and forces the other parties to defend them, the party must pay realistic litigation costs.

issues.legal_issue: An allegation that an environmental report was fabricated does not establish contempt when the record shows that the filed report was the final report and there is no basis for the allegation.
material_facts: The applicants alleged that the pollution control authority had fabricated or altered an expert report filed in court.
The expert institution’s acting director stated that the filed document was a copy of its final report.
The allegation appeared to rely on a comparison with a draft report inspected at the expert institution, and the record disclosed no basis to find fabrication.
issues.conclusion: The court found no basis for the fabrication allegation and dismissed the contempt application as without merit.
issues.legal_principle: A contempt allegation based on fabrication requires a factual basis showing that the filed material was fabricated or altered; an allegation alone is insufficient. The court relied on the record and the expert institution’s affidavit identifying the filed document as a copy of its final report.

predicates.contempt_proceeding_alleging_report_fabr: A party brought a contempt proceeding alleging that a report filed in court had been fabricated.
predicates.filed_document_identified_as_final_repor: The institution that prepared the report identified the filed document as a copy of its final report.
predicates.no_evidence_of_fabrication: The record did not provide a factual basis for finding that the report had been fabricated.

issues.definition: In a contempt proceeding alleging report fabrication, identifying the filed document as the final report and lacking evidence of fabrication means the contempt allegation is not established.
